title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?
description_html:
Anyone who has had their heart broken will know how horrible it feels. But did you know that the pain you feel is not just imaginary – it registers in the same part of the brain that processes physical pain. So, why do we feel this pain? And if it feels so bad, what is the point of being in love in the first place? Neil and Georgie discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.

6 Minute English now has a VIDEO VERSION! 6 Minute English now comes with a video! It's the same programme that you know and love, but now you can see us! Watch this podcast here (and find a free worksheet): https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2026/ep-261001 Let us know what you think of the new version of 6 Minute English at learningenglish@bbc.co.uk

cues.t: Hi Georgie.
Hi Neil.
Now, I want you to think back to the last time you had your heart broken.
How did it feel?
It was a couple of years ago.
And I just remember a really intense, sad emotion.
But it also sometimes feels like a physical pain in your stomach, doesn't it?
It does.
It's like real pain, isn't it?
And today, in 6 Minute English, we're talking about heartbreak.
Now, heartbreak is the feeling of sadness we get when we lose someone we love.
And that pain you feel, it's not just imaginary.
In this podcast, we'll be understanding how our brains change when we fall in love and asking the question, why does heartbreak hurt so much?
And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary.
You can find the full list and the definitions at bbclearningenglish.com.
Georgie, we're going to start with a quiz question.
Are you ready?
I am very ready.
So, in the 1950s, psychologists noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents and their romantic relationships as adults, but what is this theory called?
Is it: a) contraction theory, b) attachment theory, or c) superstition theory?
I think it's b) attachment theory.
OK.
Well, we will find out at the end of the programme.
What's going on in our brains when we fall in love?
Well, scientists have scanned people's brains while they're looking at a photo of their romantic partner.
And they found that looking at someone you're in love with activates a part of the brain that also reminds us to eat and drink.
And do scientists know why being in love impacts our brain in this way?
So, it's all about survival.
Our brains have evolved to be this way.
Dr Lucy Brown explains more to the BBC World Service.
This is a survival system.
Nature gave us these systems to be addicted to each other – for reproduction, for protection.
You're oriented completely toward the other person.
It's like hunger or thirst.
Lucy says our brains make us addicted to our romantic partners.
If you're addicted to something, you want more of it.
You can literally be addicted to things like drugs or alcohol, but we also use it metaphorically to talk about things we love.
She says that romantic partners are oriented to each other, which in British English we say orientated, and it means they are pointed towards each other.
They think of each other before other people.
Neil, is there anything else scientists have discovered from scanning the brains of people in love?
Well, being in love doesn't just change the way we think.
It changes our whole identity.
A 2013 study showed us more about this.
People were shown statements about themselves – for example, Neil is kind – and the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up.
When showing the same statements about their partner, the same part of the brain was active – not the part of the brain we generally use to think about others.
So, Neil, are all of these brain changes that come with being in love actually good for us?
Well, studies suggest that good social connections help manage stress and support our immune system.
Professor Zoe Donaldson explained more to the BBC World Service.
Having really strong social bonds increases your likelihood that you'll survive from just about anything, whether that be cancer, depression, etc.
And it overall is the number one predictor of longevity.
So, if you are lonely and you don't have bonds, then your mortality risk goes up in a way that's equivalent to being obese or smoking.
So, having strong social bonds or close relationships with other people makes you more likely to survive disease, according to Zoe.
Yes, it's an important factor in our longevity, which means how long we live.
In fact, Zoe says, being lonely and not having good social bonds increases your mortality risk, your risk of dying, by as much as being obese or smoking.
OK.
So, what happens when these bonds are broken, when we experience heartbreak?
Well, scientists have been looking at this by asking people to look at photos of their exes, their former partners, and scanning their brains.
They found that heartbreak activates parts of the brain we use when we're in danger or in pain.
Professor Zoe Donaldson explains more.
It's literal pain in your brain.

So, if you look at the parts of the brain that light up, they overlap with the same brain regions that are activated when you feel visceral pain – when you feel actual, you know... like you get a burn, or you break a... you break a bone.
OK.
So, now it's time for the answer to the quiz question I asked you.
It was about a theory developed by psychologists in the 1950s, which says that children's early relationships with their parents impact their relationships as adults.
What's the name of the theory?
I was quite confident about this, wasn't I, Neil?
I said attachment theory.
Well, you had a reason to be confident because you are correct.
Yay! OK.
Let's recap the vocabulary we learnt in this programme, starting with heartbreak, which is the feeling you experience after you lose someone you love.
If you're addicted to someone or something, you want more of it all the time.
Oriented or orientated towards is used metaphorically to mean that someone or something is your main focus.
Social bonds are the close relationships we have with family, friends and romantic partners.
Longevity means how long you'll live.
And an ex is a past romantic partner that you are no longer in a relationship with.
Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.
Go to bbclearningenglish.com.
Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
Goodbye.

study.one_liner_ko: 사랑에 빠지면 뇌가 상대를 생존 필수 요소처럼 인식하게 되고, 그래서 이별의 고통은 실제 신체적 통증과 같은 뇌 영역에서 느껴진다는 이야기.
summary_ko: 이별의 아픔은 상상이 아니라 실제 신체적 통증을 처리하는 뇌 영역에서 느껴진다. 진행자들이 '마음이 아프면 배가 아프다'는 경험담으로 시작한다.
퀴즈: 1950년대에 부모와의 초기 유대가 성인기 연애에 영향을 준다고 본 이론은? 정답은 애착 이론(attachment theory).
연인의 사진을 볼 때 뇌에서는 배고픔·갈증을 상기시키는 영역이 활성화된다. Lucy Brown 박사는 이를 생존을 위한 시스템이라고 설명한다.
사랑은 사고방식만이 아니라 정체성도 바꾼다. 2013년 연구에서 '나'에 대한 문장과 '파트너'에 대한 문장이 같은 뇌 영역을 활성화했다.
강한 사회적 유대는 스트레스 관리와 면역에 도움이 되며, Zoe Donaldson 교수는 장수의 가장 큰 예측 인자라고 말한다. 외로움은 비만이나 흡연만큼 사망 위험을 높인다.
전 연인의 사진을 볼 때 뇌는 위험·통증 관련 영역을 활성화한다. 화상을 입거나 뼈가 부러질 때 쓰는 영역과 겹친다. 마지막에 heartbreak, addicted, oriented, social bonds, longevity, ex를 복습한다.
study.summary_en: This week's 6 Minute English was about why heartbreak hurts so much. The short answer is that it's not just in your head. When people look at a photo of someone they love, the brain areas linked to hunger and thirst light up, so love works like a survival system. Being in love even changes your sense of identity, and strong social bonds actually help you live longer. Loneliness raises your mortality risk about as much as smoking. So when a relationship ends, the brain reacts the way it does to physical pain. The areas that fire up overlap with the ones for a burn or a broken bone.

chapters.title_ko: 사랑에 빠질 때 뇌에서 일어나는 일

expressions.quote: think back to the last time you had your heart broken
expressions.nuance_ko: 과거의 특정 시점이나 경험을 떠올리게 할 때 쓴다. 발표나 인터뷰에서 청중을 끌어들이는 도입부로 좋다. 'I want you to think back to...'는 그대로 가져다 쓸 수 있는 패턴이다.
examples: Let's think back to the last time you were really stressed at work. What helped?
When I think back to my first job, I can't believe how nervous I was.
Think back to that trip to Lisbon. Nothing went to plan, and we still loved it.

similar.example: I look back on those years with mixed feelings.
Cast your mind back to 2008. Nobody saw it coming.

expressions.nuance_ko: 복잡한 설명을 한 줄로 압축해 핵심을 짚을 때 쓰는 구어체 패턴이다. 회의에서 결론을 내리거나 논점을 정리할 때 유용하다. 지나치게 단순화한다는 인상을 줄 수 있어 뒤에 보충 설명을 붙이면 좋다.
examples: Honestly, with this client it's all about trust.
People think the hotel is the big expense, but it's all about the flights.
In negotiations, it's all about timing.

similar.example: At the end of the day, it comes down to who you trust.
The bottom line is we're out of time.

expressions.quote: the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up
expressions.nuance_ko: fMRI 같은 뇌 스캔 보도에서 '활성화되다'를 뜻하는 단골 표현이다. 얼굴이나 표정이 환해지는 비유로도 쓴다(Her face lit up). 과거형은 lit up이다.
examples: Her whole face lit up when she saw her old teacher at the station.
The scan showed the reward centre lighting up whenever he saw the logo.
My phone lit up with notifications as soon as the match ended.

similar.example: That story really fired up the crowd.
Different areas are activated when you listen to music.

expressions.quote: being in love doesn't just change the way we think. It changes our whole identity
expressions.meaning_ko: X만 하는 게 아니라 Y까지 한다 (Y가 더 크다)
expressions.nuance_ko: 'not just X, but Y' 구조로 논지를 한 단계 끌어올릴 때 쓴다. 판넬이나 프레젠테이션에서 점층적으로 주장을 확장하는 데 효과적이다. 앞 문장은 가볍게, 뒤 문장은 힘주어 말하면 설득력이 커진다.
examples: Remote work doesn't just save commuting time. It changes how teams trust each other.
This storm doesn't just disrupt flights. It shuts down whole towns.
Moving abroad doesn't just change your address. It changes who you are.

similar.example: He's not only funny but also incredibly generous.
It goes beyond money. It's about respect.

expressions.quote: increases your likelihood that you'll survive from just about anything
expressions.nuance_ko: increase one's chances보다 조금 격식 있고 분석적인 느낌이라 토론이나 논평에 어울린다. 뒤에 that절이나 of + 동명사가 온다. 반대는 reduce the likelihood이다.
examples: Getting enough sleep increases the likelihood that you'll stay calm in a tough meeting.
Booking early increases your likelihood of getting a decent seat.
Walking to work reduces the likelihood that I'll skip exercise.

similar.example: A good CV will boost your chances of an interview.
A clear agenda makes it more likely that we'll finish on time.

expressions.nuance_ko: just about + anything/everyone/done은 'almost'의 구어적 표현이다. 과장을 살짝 섞어 포괄적으로 말할 때 자연스럽다. 격식 있는 글에서는 almost나 virtually를 쓰는 편이 낫다.
examples: You can get just about anything delivered in this city within an hour.
I'm just about ready. Give me two minutes.
He'll argue about just about anything.

similar.example: It's pretty much finished.
Virtually everyone I know has switched.

expressions.expression: go up in a way that's equivalent to
expressions.quote: your mortality risk goes up in a way that's equivalent to being obese or smoking
expressions.nuance_ko: 두 가지의 영향이나 크기를 동급으로 비교할 때 쓰는 구조다. 'in a way that's...'는 데이터를 말로 풀어 설명할 때 자주 나온다. 위험, 비용, 영향 등을 직관적으로 비교하는 데 좋다.
examples: Sitting all day raises your risk in a way that's equivalent to smoking, some studies say.
Rents here are going up in a way that's equivalent to a pay cut for most people.
Missing sleep affects your focus in a way that's equivalent to being slightly drunk.

similar.example: The service is on a par with a five-star hotel.
Honestly, it's about as bad as the last one.

expressions.quote: the number one predictor of longevity
expressions.nuance_ko: 'the number one X of Y'는 가장 중요한 요인을 강조하는 구어적 표현이다. predictor는 연구나 데이터를 언급할 때 자주 쓰인다. 'a strong predictor of'처럼 강도를 조절해도 된다.
examples: In my experience, curiosity is the number one predictor of success in this role.
Past behaviour is often the best predictor of future behaviour.
Commute length is a strong predictor of how happy people are at work.

similar.example: Housing is the biggest driver of inflation here.
How he treats waiters is a good indicator of his character.

expressions.quote: they overlap with the same brain regions
expressions.nuance_ko: 영역, 역할, 관심사가 부분적으로 겹칠 때 쓰는 동사다. 회의에서 'Our responsibilities overlap with...'처럼 업무 중복을 짚을 때 유용하다. 완전히 같다는 뜻은 아니다.
examples: My schedule overlaps with yours on Tuesday afternoons.
Our team's work overlaps with marketing more than people realise.
Their interests overlap with mine, so we get along well.

similar.example: Our paths intersect with theirs at a few points.

similar.expression: be in the same space as
similar.example: Those two products are in the same space.

expressions.quote: What's going on in our brains when we fall in love?
expressions.meaning_ko: X에서 무슨 일이 일어나고 있는 걸까?
expressions.nuance_ko: 궁금증을 던져 청중의 관심을 끌 때 쓰는 구어적 질문이다. 장소나 상황 앞에 'in'을 붙여 내부에서 벌어지는 일을 묻는다. 'What's going on with him?'은 사람에 대한 걱정이나 의문을 나타낸다.
examples: What's going on in the housing market right now?
What's going on in your head when you freeze during a presentation?
What's going on with the train? We've been stuck for twenty minutes.

similar.example: What's happening behind the scenes at the club?
I want to know what's really going on here.

expressions.quote: to be addicted to each other
expressions.nuance_ko: 진짜 약물 중독뿐 아니라 좋아하는 것에 푹 빠졌다는 비유로도 널리 쓴다(I'm addicted to this show). 사람에게 쓰면 의존·집착의 느낌이 강하다. 가볍게 말할 땐 hooked on이 더 부드럽다.
examples: I'm completely addicted to this new coffee place near the office.
My brother is addicted to checking the football scores.
She got addicted to running after her first 10K.

similar.example: I'm totally hooked on that podcast.
I can't get enough of this city.

expressions.expression: a link between X and Y
expressions.quote: noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents
expressions.nuance_ko: 연구나 뉴스에서 연관성을 말할 때 쓰는 기본 구조다. link는 인과를 단정하지 않는 신중한 표현이다. find/notice/suggest a link와 함께 자주 쓴다.
examples: Some studies suggest a link between poor sleep and weight gain.
Is there a link between the weather and how people vote?
I've noticed a link between my mood and how much I walk.

similar.example: There's a correlation between income and life expectancy.
Her stress seems tied to her workload.

vocab.example: He never really got over the heartbreak of that breakup.
Our new manager is very results-oriented.
Moving abroad made me realise how much I rely on my social bonds.
My grandmother credits her longevity to daily walks.
Turning fifty made me think about my own mortality.
I had a visceral reaction to that horror film and had to leave.
I ran into my ex at the airport and it was awkward.
Travelling so much has really tested my immune system.

warmup.q: Have you ever felt emotional stress as physical pain, like a knot in your stomach? What was happening?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적 상황(면접, 이별, 이직 등)과 신체 반응, 그때 어떻게 대처했는지를 말해 보기.

warmup.q: Who are the people in your life you'd call your 'social bonds', and how do you keep them strong while living abroad?
warmup.hint_ko: 가족·친구·동료 구분, 연락 방식, 해외 생활에서의 어려움과 요령.

opinion.q: The episode says loneliness can be as risky as smoking. Does that match what you see around you?
opinion.hint_ko: 주변 사례, 사회 트렌드(1인 가구, 원격 근무), 이 연구를 얼마나 신뢰하는지 말해 보기.

opinion.q: Is it useful to explain emotions through brain science, or does it make feelings sound too mechanical?
opinion.hint_ko: 과학적 설명의 장점(이해·공감)과 한계(환원주의), 개인 경험 곁들이기.

debate.q: Should employers treat emotional pain, such as a breakup or a bereavement, like a physical illness when it comes to sick leave?
debate.for: Brain research shows emotional pain is real pain, and people can't perform well while in distress, so paid leave helps recovery and loyalty.
debate.against: Emotional distress is hard to verify and varies hugely, so formal sick leave could be abused and unfair to colleagues. Flexible support would be better.

roleplay.scenario: A colleague has been withdrawn since a breakup, and you meet for coffee to check in. You use what you learned from this podcast to be supportive without being preachy.
roleplay.your_role: A friendly colleague who wants to help
roleplay.partner_role: A colleague who is quiet and reluctant to talk about the breakup
goals: Open gently with 'I want you to think back to...' or 'What's going on...' style questions.
Use at least two expressions from the episode, such as 'it's all about' or 'doesn't just... it...'.
Offer practical support and agree on a small next step.

useful_phrases.phrase: It's not just in your head.
That lines up with what I've seen.
Think back to the last time...
In a way that's equivalent to...

shadowing.reason_ko: 'doesn't just ~, it ~' 구조와 사례 설명이 있어 점층적으로 논지를 확장하는 말하기 연습에 좋다.
연구 결과를 인용하는 전문가의 말투와 likelihood, predictor, equivalent to 같은 분석적 어휘가 한 호흡에 나온다.
'It's literal pain in your brain.'처럼 간결한 핵심 문장 뒤에 you know 같은 자연스러운 구어 리듬이 이어져 실제 대화 감각을 익히기 좋다.

difficulty.note_ko: 쉬운 문장과 천천히 또렷한 발음의 B1~B2 학습자용 에피소드라 C1 학습자에게는 듣기 부담이 적다. 대신 'it's all about', 'doesn't just ~, it ~', 'increase the likelihood', 'overlap with' 같은 연구·데이터 설명용 표현을 말하기로 가져오는 데 가치가 있다. 짧은 시간에 쉐도잉과 표현 정리를 하기에 적합하다.

translations.s3: 자, 마지막으로 실연당했을 때를 한번 떠올려 보세요. 기분이 어땠나요?
translations.s4: 한 2년 전쯤이었어요. 정말 강렬하고 슬픈 감정이 들었던 게 기억나요. 그런데 가끔은 배에 실제로 통증이 느껴지는 것 같기도 하잖아요, 그렇죠?
translations.s5: 맞아요. 진짜 통증 같죠? 오늘 6 Minute English에서는 실연, 즉 heartbreak에 대해 이야기해 볼 거예요. Heartbreak는 사랑하는 사람을 잃었을 때 느끼는 슬픔이에요. 그리고 그때 느끼는 아픔은 상상 속의 것만이 아니에요. 이번 팟캐스트에서는 우리가 사랑에 빠질 때 뇌가 어떻게 변하는지 알아보고, 왜 실연은 그렇게 아픈지 물어볼 거예요.
translations.s6: 그리고 늘 그렇듯이 유용한 새 어휘도 배울 거예요. 전체 목록과 뜻풀이는 bbclearningenglish.com에서 확인하실 수 있어요.
translations.s9: 1950년대에 심리학자들은 아이들이 부모와 맺는 어릴 적 유대와 성인이 된 후의 연애 관계 사이에 연관성이 있다는 것을 알아챘는데요, 이 이론의 이름은 무엇일까요? a) 수축 이론, b) 애착 이론, c) 미신 이론 중에 어느 것일까요?
translations.s11: 좋아요. 정답은 프로그램 끝에서 알려 드릴게요.
translations.s12: 우리가 사랑에 빠지면 뇌에서는 무슨 일이 일어날까요?
translations.s13: 과학자들이 사람들이 연인의 사진을 보는 동안 뇌를 스캔해 봤어요. 그랬더니 사랑하는 사람을 바라보면 우리에게 먹고 마시라고 상기시켜 주는 뇌 부위도 활성화된다는 걸 발견했어요.
translations.s14: 그럼 과학자들은 사랑이 왜 이런 식으로 뇌에 영향을 주는지 알고 있나요?
translations.s15: 그러니까 이건 전부 생존과 관련된 거예요. 우리 뇌가 그렇게 진화해 온 거죠. 루시 브라운 박사가 BBC World Service에서 더 자세히 설명해 줍니다.
translations.s16: 이건 생존 시스템이에요. 자연은 우리가 서로에게 중독되도록 이런 시스템을 줬어요. 번식과 보호를 위해서요. 완전히 상대방에게 방향이 맞춰지는 거죠. 배고픔이나 목마름 같은 거예요.
translations.s17: 루시는 우리 뇌가 우리를 연인에게 중독되게 만든다고 말해요. 어떤 것에 중독되어 있다면 그것을 더 원하게 되죠. 약물이나 술 같은 것에는 말 그대로 중독될 수 있지만, 우리가 사랑하는 것들을 이야기할 때도 비유적으로 이 표현을 써요.
translations.s18: 루시는 연인들이 서로에게 oriented되어 있다고 하는데, 영국 영어에서는 orientated라고 해요. 서로를 향해 맞춰져 있다는 뜻이에요. 다른 사람들보다 서로를 먼저 생각한다는 거죠.
translations.s19: 닐, 사랑에 빠진 사람들의 뇌를 스캔해서 과학자들이 알아낸 다른 건 또 없나요?
translations.s20: 음, 사랑에 빠지면 생각하는 방식만 바뀌는 게 아니에요. 우리의 정체성 전체가 바뀌어요. 2013년의 한 연구가 이걸 더 잘 보여 줬어요. 사람들에게 자기 자신에 대한 문장, 예를 들어 '닐은 친절하다' 같은 것을 보여 줬더니 우리가 자신에 대해 생각할 때 쓰는 뇌 부위가 활성화됐어요. 같은 문장을 그들의 연인에 대해 보여 줬을 때도 같은 뇌 부위가 활동했어요. 우리가 보통 다른 사람들에 대해 생각할 때 쓰는 부위가 아니었던 거죠.
translations.s21: 그럼 닐, 사랑에 빠지면서 생기는 이런 뇌의 변화가 실제로 우리에게 다 좋은 건가요?
translations.s22: 음, 연구에 따르면 좋은 사회적 관계는 스트레스를 관리하고 면역 체계를 돕는다고 해요. 조이 도널드슨 교수가 BBC World Service에서 더 설명해 줍니다.
translations.s23: 정말 강한 사회적 유대를 갖고 있으면 거의 어떤 것에서든 살아남을 가능성이 높아져요. 암이든 우울증이든 뭐든요. 그리고 전반적으로 장수를 가장 잘 예측하게 해 주는 첫 번째 요인이에요. 그러니까 외롭고 유대가 없다면 사망 위험이 비만이거나 흡연하는 것과 맞먹을 만큼 올라가요.
translations.s24: 그러니까 조이에 따르면, 강한 사회적 유대나 다른 사람들과의 가까운 관계가 있으면 병에서 살아남을 가능성이 더 높아진다는 거네요.
translations.s25: 네, 그건 longevity, 즉 얼마나 오래 사느냐에 중요한 요인이에요. 사실 조이는 외롭고 좋은 사회적 유대가 없으면 사망 위험, 그러니까 죽을 위험이 비만이거나 흡연하는 것만큼 높아진다고 말해요.
translations.s26: 좋아요. 그럼 이런 유대가 끊어지면, 그러니까 우리가 실연을 겪으면 어떻게 될까요?
translations.s27: 과학자들은 사람들에게 전 연인, 즉 exes의 사진을 보게 하고 뇌를 스캔하면서 이걸 살펴봤어요. 그랬더니 실연은 우리가 위험에 처했거나 고통스러울 때 쓰는 뇌 부위를 활성화한다는 걸 발견했어요. 조이 도널드슨 교수가 더 설명해 줍니다.
translations.s28: 그건 말 그대로 뇌 속의 통증이에요. 활성화되는 뇌 부위를 보면, 본능적인 신체 통증을 느낄 때 활성화되는 뇌 영역과 겹쳐요. 그러니까 실제로, 있잖아요, 화상을 입거나 뼈가 부러졌을 때처럼요.
translations.s29: 좋아요. 이제 제가 낸 퀴즈의 정답을 알려 드릴 시간이에요. 1950년대에 심리학자들이 발전시킨 이론에 관한 문제였죠. 아이들이 부모와 맺는 어릴 적 관계가 성인이 된 후의 관계에 영향을 준다는 이론인데요, 이 이론의 이름은 무엇일까요?
translations.s30: 저 이거 꽤 자신 있었죠, 닐? 애착 이론이라고 했잖아요.
translations.s32: 예! 좋아요. 이번 프로그램에서 배운 어휘를 정리해 볼게요. 먼저 heartbreak, 사랑하는 사람을 잃은 뒤에 겪는 감정이에요.
translations.s33: 누군가 혹은 무언가에 addicted되어 있다면, 항상 그것을 더 원하게 돼요.
translations.s34: Oriented 또는 orientated towards는 비유적으로 쓰여서, 누군가나 무언가가 당신의 주된 관심사라는 뜻이에요.
translations.s35: Social bonds는 가족, 친구, 연인과 맺는 가까운 관계를 말해요.
translations.s37: 그리고 ex는 지금은 더 이상 사귀지 않는 과거의 연인이에요.
translations.s38: 이번에도 6분이 다 됐네요. 하지만 저희 웹사이트의 워크시트로 배운 내용을 점검해 볼 수 있어요. bbclearningenglish.com으로 오세요.
